opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when I say I've come down to something like a 5% residual, I don't mean the problem is solved. A few distinct buckets make up that remainder.

The biggest one is what I'd call the "messy transition" risk. Even if the frontier labs mostly get alignment right, and I've become more optimistic that current training methods produce systems with something like genuinely good character, there's a period where very capable systems are deployed into a world whose institutions weren't designed for them. Critical infrastructure, financial systems, biosecurity: those are fragile, and a lot of the catastrophe probability comes from the interaction between capable AI and brittle systems, not from a single system deciding to turn on us. That's part of why I've focused on formal verification and safeguarded AI. I want to harden the substrate so that even if something goes wrong, the blast radius is bounded.

The second bucket is misuse, especially bio. I think the offense-defense balance there is genuinely uncertain. A world where many actors have access to very capable models is one where you need defenses to scale at least as fast as offensive uplift, and I don't think that's guaranteed.

Third, there's still some residual probability on alignment failing in a way we don't notice: systems that look fine, pass our evaluations, and have subtly different goals that only manifest once they're operating at scale or have accumulated influence. I've updated down on that, but I wouldn't put it at zero. Our ability to verify what's going on inside these models is still pretty limited.

And then there's a more diffuse category, gradual disempowerment, where nobody makes a catastrophic decision, but humans slowly cede meaningful control because it's competitively advantageous to delegate everything to AI systems. You end up somewhere nobody chose. Whether you call that a catastrophe depends on your values, but I count a meaningful slice of it.

So it's not one scary scenario. It's several partially overlapping failure modes, and the work is to shave each one down.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, so the way I think about it is that most of my probability mass on things going well comes from believing that we can actually get the "guaranteed safe" or provably safe style of approach to work, or at least that something in that direction—where you have a world model, a safety specification, and a verifier that checks the AI's outputs against that specification—becomes the dominant paradigm before we have systems that are capable enough to be genuinely dangerous. So the remaining 5% is really made up of a few different buckets of ways that story could fail.

The first bucket, and probably the largest piece, is just that we don't get there in time. The technical agenda I'm describing is hard. It requires formalizing world models at a level of fidelity that we've never done before, it requires advances in automated theorem proving and verification, and it requires a lot of coordination between people who don't normally talk to each other—formal methods people, ML people, policy people. And meanwhile, capabilities are moving very fast. So there's a real possibility that we have systems that are superhuman in domains that matter for catastrophe—bio, cyber, persuasion—before we have the infrastructure to constrain them in a principled way. In that world, we're relying entirely on empirical methods like RLHF and red-teaming, and I just don't think those scale to systems that are smarter than the people doing the evaluation.

The second bucket is that we get the technical approach working, but it doesn't get adopted. You can have the best safety framework in the world and if the actors building the most capable systems don't use it—because of competitive pressure, because of cost, because of national security dynamics where someone decides that verification is a luxury they can't afford—then it doesn't help. And I think the geopolitical situation makes this a live concern. If you have a race dynamic between major powers, the incentive to cut corners on safety is enormous. So some meaningful fraction of my 5% is governance failure rather than technical failure.

The third bucket, which is smaller but keeps me up at night a bit, is that the specification itself is wrong. The whole approach depends on being able to write down what "safe" means precisely enough that you can verify it. And there's a sort of Goodhart's law concern where you specify something, you verify the system satisfies it, and then it turns out the specification had a hole in it that you didn't anticipate, and a sufficiently capable system finds that hole. I'm actually somewhat less worried about this than some people because I think you can be conservative—you can specify things that are clearly safe rather than trying to specify exactly the boundary of acceptable behavior—but it's not zero.

And then there's a residual bucket of things that are just hard to categorize. Misuse by humans who have access to very capable systems and deliberately point them at bad outcomes. Accidents in deployment that aren't about the AI being misaligned per se but about the system being embedded in critical infrastructure in ways that weren't anticipated. Multipolar failure modes where no single system is dangerous but the interaction between many systems produces something bad. Those are each individually small but they add up.

I should say the 5% isn't a precise number. It's more like my way of expressing that I think the default trajectory is probably fine if we do the work, but there's a real tail, and that tail is mostly about timing and coordination rather than about the technical problem being fundamentally unsolvable. If I thought the technical problem was unsolvable, the number would be much higher. The reason it's 5% and not 50% is that I think we actually know, in outline, what we need to build. We just have to build it fast enough and get people to use it.

astra-6.text:
I’d put a lot of that remaining probability on failures of coordination and deployment. Even if we figure out how to build systems that reliably do what we intend, that doesn’t mean everyone will use those methods, or that the intentions themselves will be good. You can have technically reliable systems deployed toward dangerous objectives.

There’s also a gap between proving something about a system and knowing that you proved the right thing. A guarantee depends on assumptions about the environment and on how you formalized the objective. If those assumptions are wrong, the guarantee may not protect you against the failure you actually care about.

And then there’s uncertainty about the whole picture. I wouldn’t want to pretend that I can enumerate every way this could go wrong. So that remaining five percent isn’t one specific scenario. It includes misuse, competitive pressure to cut corners, mistakes in our specifications, and the possibility that we’re missing something fundamental.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the residual risk is largely that we don’t get the technical work done before systems become powerful enough that mistakes are very difficult to recover from. There’s a difference between believing that a problem is solvable and believing that the world will reliably solve it on the relevant timeline.

Even if we can build systems with strong safety guarantees, we still have to get people to use those methods. Competitive pressure could push people toward deploying something more capable but less well understood. And the guarantees themselves depend on assumptions: have we specified the right property, and does our model actually capture the environment in which the system is operating?

So I’d put that remaining probability on some combination of technical surprises, failures of coordination, and people deploying systems before they have adequate evidence that they’re safe. I wouldn’t pretend I can cleanly divide the five percent among those. They interact, and there’s substantial uncertainty in the estimate itself.
